The oracle's core, “for the battle is not yours, but God's” and “you will not need to fight this battle” (אַ֠תֶּם אַל תִּֽירְא֤וּ וְאַל תֵּחַ֨תּוּ֙ מִפְּנֵ֨י הֶהָמ֤וֹן הָרָב֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י לֹ֥א לָכֶ֛ם הַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה כִּ֥י לֵאלֹהִֽים; לֹ֥א לָכֶ֖ם לְהִלָּחֵ֣ם בָּזֹ֑את), is answered immediately, without narrative gap, by Jehoshaphat's prostration, “he bowed his head with his face to the ground” (וַיִּקֹּ֧ד יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט אַפַּ֖יִם אָ֑רְצָה), and the Levites' praise “with an exceedingly loud voice” (לְהַלֵּ֗ל לַיהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּק֥וֹל גָּד֖וֹל לְמָֽעְלָה); per the inset rule the response stays inside the oracle's own unit since nothing frames it as resumed narrative. The next verse resets with a new day and place, “they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa” (וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֵּצְא֖וּ לְמִדְבַּ֣ר תְּק֑וֹעַ), which is the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting the oracle (14-17) from the worship response (18-19) into two rows would sever the response from the very deliverance it thanks God for in advance, contrary to the inset rule's both-sides-framed test.

boundary_rationale: The march begins with the new-day formula that closed the previous row's argument (וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֵּצְא֖וּ לְמִדְבַּ֣ר תְּק֑וֹעַ), and Jehoshaphat's second speech, “…Believe in Yahweh your God, so you will be established! Believe his prophets, so you will prosper” (הַאֲמִ֜ינוּ בַּיהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם֙ וְתֵ֣אָמֵ֔נוּ הַאֲמִ֥ינוּ בִנְבִיאָ֖יו וְהַצְלִֽיחוּ), sets up the singers who go out crying “give thanks to Yahweh, for his loving kindness endures forever” (וְאֹֽמְרִים֙ הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֔ה כִּ֥י לְעוֹלָ֖ם חַסְדּֽוֹ), the hymn line that triggers Yahweh's ambush against the coalition, “Yahweh set ambushers against the children of Ammon” (נָתַ֣ן יְהוָ֣ה מְ֠אָֽרְבִים עַל בְּנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן), and their mutual slaughter, “…everyone helped to destroy each other” (עָזְר֥וּ אִישׁ בְּרֵעֵ֖הוּ לְמַשְׁחִֽית). The causally connected discovery of corpses, “behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and there were none who escaped” (וְהִנָּ֧ם פְּגָרִ֛ים נֹפְלִ֥ים אַ֖רְצָה וְאֵ֥ין פְּלֵיטָֽה), belongs to the same chain as the plunderers of v.25, “Jehoshaphat and his people” (יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט וְעַמּוֹ֮), the Beracah etiology, “…the name of that place was called “Beracah Valley” to this day” (עַל כֵּ֡ן קָֽרְא֞וּ אֶת שֵׁ֨ם הַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֛וּא עֵ֥מֶק בְּרָכָ֖ה עַד הַיּֽוֹם), the doubled-return notice that follows it, “Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat in front of them, to go again to Jerusalem with joy; for Yahweh had made them to rejoice over their enemies” (וַ֠יָּשֻׁבוּ כָּל אִ֨ישׁ יְהוּדָ֤ה וִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט בְּרֹאשָׁ֔ם לָשׁ֥וּב אֶל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בְּשִׂמְחָ֑ה כִּֽי שִׂמְּחָ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה מֵֽאוֹיְבֵיהֶֽם, v.27) and their temple arrival with instruments (וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם בִּנְבָלִ֥ים וּבְכִנֹּר֖וֹת וּבַחֲצֹצְר֑וֹת אֶל בֵּ֖ית יְהוָֽה, v.28) -- a figura etymologica on the returning root -- the bare infinitive, without conjunctive prefix, stands only here at 20:27; the vav-prefixed form recurs at 30:9, a different unpointed string, not an identical word-form repetition -- and this finite-plus-cognate-infinitive pairing is itself unique to 20:27 book-wide. It shares its device-class with 19:1's own return notice, but functions here as the still-unfolding aftermath of the very battle just narrated rather than 19:1's pivot to a wholly new scene and participant (Jehu, the rebuke): the fear-of-nations (v.29) and rest-formula (v.30) that follow are direct consequences of this war, not a fresh initiative, which is why the device does not drive a split here the way it does at 19:1 -- the surrounding nations' dread, “the fear of God was on all the kingdoms of the countries” (וַיְהִי֙ פַּ֣חַד אֱלֹהִ֔ים עַ֖ל כָּל מַמְלְכ֣וֹת הָאֲרָצ֑וֹת), and the closing rest-formula, “the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around” (וַתִּשְׁקֹ֖ט מַלְכ֣וּת יְהוֹשָׁפָ֑ט וַיָּ֧נַֽח ל֦וֹ אֱלֹהָ֖יו מִסָּבִֽיב) — a PE, single-witness, marks the close here. Verse 31 breaks decisively into the reign's age-and-length notice, “…בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים֩ וְחָמֵ֨שׁ שָׁנָ֜ה…” (“thirty-five years old”), a formula with no place in the narrative just closed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the battle proper (20-24) from the plunder-to-rest sequence (25-30) would cut the chain at its weakest visible joint; no formula or mark falls there, and although the grammatical subject NP does shift, from v.24's collective וִֽיהוּדָ֛ה בָּ֥א ("Judah came") to v.25's named-plus-collective וַיָּבֹ֨א יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט וְעַמּוֹ֮ ("Jehoshaphat and his people came"), the plunderers of v.25 are referentially the same body as v.24's Judah, so continuity here is a matter of reference, not grammar -- the row is kept whole despite its length, at correspondingly reduced confidence.

boundary_rationale: The rest-formula that just closed the war narrative yields to the reign's own accession notice, “Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah; he was thirty-five years old when he began to reign” (וַיִּמְלֹ֥ךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט עַל יְהוּדָ֑ה בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים֩ וְחָמֵ֨שׁ שָׁנָ֜ה בְּמָלְכ֗וֹ), followed by evaluation formulas, “he walked in the way of Asa his father, and didn't turn away from it” (וַיֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּדֶ֛רֶךְ אָבִ֥יו אָסָ֖א וְלֹא סָ֣ר מִמֶּ֑נָּה), qualified by the concessive “however the high places were not taken away” (אַ֥ךְ הַבָּמ֖וֹת לֹא סָ֑רוּ). The unit closes on the source-citation formula, “the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last…are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani” (וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֔ט הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים בְּדִבְרֵי֙ יֵה֣וּא בֶן חֲנָ֔נִי), a pattern attested at reign-closes elsewhere in the book (e.g. 13:22, 25:26, 26:22); notably, the historian named here is the same Jehu ben Hanani who confronted the king in person at the opening of this part (19:2), closing this reign's record with the prophetic voice that had opened it. Verse 35 reopens the narrative register with a fresh time-marker, “After this, Jehoshaphat…joined himself with Ahaziah…” (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן אֶתְחַבַּר֙ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה עִ֖ם אֲחַזְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ה֖וּא הִרְשִׁ֥יעַ לַעֲשֽׂוֹת), showing the source-citation closed only this evaluative block, not the reign's remaining material.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through v.37 on the grounds that the reign is not formally over until 21:1 misreads the source-citation as all-inclusive; the formula closes a sub-unit of the reign's record here, not the reign itself, so further appended material can and does follow.

boundary_rationale: A second “after this” marker reopens narrative time, sharing the אחרי כן idiom that opened the Moabite crisis at 20:1 (וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן, a wayyiqtol-of-hayah frame) though in the lighter construction וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן (a bare conjunctive waw directly on the adverbial, no preposed וַיְהִי): “Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel. The same did very wickedly” (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן אֶתְחַבַּר֙ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה עִ֖ם אֲחַזְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ה֖וּא הִרְשִׁ֥יעַ לַעֲשֽׂוֹת). A book-wide sweep of אחרי כן finds five instances -- the wayyiqtol-headed type at 20:1 and 24:4, this lighter bare-waw type at 20:35 and, inside Manasseh's own reign account rather than at any major-unit opening, 33:14, and the unrelated verse-final idiom (prepositioned form, 'from then on') at 32:23 -- so the reopened-narrative-time reading rests on the shared idiom and on 20:34's own source-citation closure and the moral-verdict register change into the Tarshish venture, not on formula identity with 20:1. The Tarshish-ships venture, “to make ships to go to Tarshish” (לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת אֳנִיּ֖וֹת לָלֶ֣כֶת תַּרְשִׁ֑ישׁ), draws Eliezer ben Dodavahu's judgment oracle, “Eliezer…prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying” (וַיִּתְנַבֵּ֞א אֱלִיעֶ֤זֶר בֶּן דֹּדָוָ֨הוּ֙ מִמָּ֣רֵשָׁ֔ה עַל יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט לֵאמֹ֑ר), whose immediate fulfillment closes this unit and this part, “the ships were wrecked, so that they were not able to go to Tarshish” (וַיִּשָּׁבְר֣וּ אֳנִיּ֔וֹת וְלֹ֥א עָצְר֖וּ לָלֶ֥כֶת אֶל תַּרְשִֽׁישׁ). The following verse breaks into an entirely different formula-class, the death-and-succession notice “Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers” (וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יְהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו), attested at reign-ends throughout the book as a two-member type completed by a proper succession clause -- 9:31's וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ רְחַבְעָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, 12:16's וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲבִיָּ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, and 27:9's fuller three-clause form וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יוֹתָם֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָחָ֥ז בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו -- which both closes Jehoshaphat's story properly and opens Jehoram's accession, a different subject taking the throne, outside this part's range.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 21:1 into this unit because both concern the aftermath of Jehoshaphat's reign ignores that the death formula is an independently recurring closer that itself begins Jehoram's accession, so the true reign-boundary falls after v.37, not after v.1 of ch.21.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the paired death-and-enthronement notice: “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב” (“slept,” i.e. died) answered by “וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹרָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Jehoram his son reigned in his place”), matching WEB 21:1 “Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers...and Jehoram his son reigned in his place” - the standard death-plus-succession opener, and also the seam-out point for the prior part. Verses 2-3 (WEB: brothers given gifts and fortified cities, but the kingdom to the firstborn) supply the family background that the purge in v4 requires. The unit closes on Jehoram's own consolidation of power: “וַיָּ֨קָם יְהוֹרָ֜ם עַל מַמְלֶ֤כַת אָבִיו֙ וַיִּתְחַזַּ֔ק וַיַּהֲרֹ֥ג אֶת כָּל אֶחָ֖יו בֶּחָ֑רֶב וְגַ֖ם מִשָּׂרֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (“Jehoram had risen up over the kingdom of his father...and killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel,” WEB 21:4). Verse 5 immediately pivots to an unrelated formulaic type (age-plus-reign-length), so v4's own narrative resolution is the natural close before that restart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through v7 to absorb the age-formula and covenant clause is the weaker reading: vv5-7 constitute a distinct, self-contained formulaic type (evaluation plus Davidic-covenant promise) rather than a continuation of the succession-and-purge narrative.

boundary_rationale: Opening edge: v5 restarts the reign account with the age formula בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וּשְׁתַּ֛יִם שָׁנָ֖ה יְהוֹרָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֑וֹ וּשְׁמוֹנֶ֣ה שָׁנִ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם ("Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem," WEB 21:5), a fixed type distinct from the narrative just closed at v4. This formula block runs through the evil-evaluation clause and the covenant-preservation promise (vv6-7), then into the accumulating 'in his days' indictment -- Edom's revolt, opening with the book's only verse-initial instance of that fronted temporal adverbial, בְּיָמָיו֙ פָּשַׁ֣ע אֱד֔וֹם ("in his days Edom revolted," v.8; the one other occurrence, MT 13:23 (= WEB 14:1)'s בְּיָמָ֛יו שָׁקְטָ֥ה הָאָ֖רֶץ, sits verse-medially), then Libnah's revolt (vv9-10). Closing edge: v11 pivots from geopolitical failure to cultic apostasy with גַּם ה֥וּא עָשָֽׂה בָמ֖וֹת בְּהָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיֶּ֨זֶן֙ אֶת יֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַיַּדַּ֖ח אֶת יְהוּדָֽה ("Moreover he made high places in the mountains of Judah, and made the inhabitants of Jerusalem play the prostitute, and led Judah astray," WEB 21:11); this is the very charge Elijah's letter indicts in vv12-13, so v11 functions as the letter's narrative antecedent and the row closes just before the letter opens. A PE (single-witness) does stand exactly at this close, at 21:11, weak and non-driving corroboration only; the nearby PE at 21:3 belongs to the preceding row's own span, not this one. The seam itself rests on the topic pivot and the letter's back-reference, with the mark as available but non-determinative support.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.8 to separate the covenant clause (5-7) from the revolt notices (8-11) is a genuine rival, not a non-issue: v.8's fronted temporal adverbial introduces a new subject, Edom -- in fact the book's only verse-initial instance of that adverbial, and so a tier-1-eligible marker by the device matrix's own time-frame-transition class. Vv.5-7 carry no 'in his days' language of their own to bracket against it. What keeps vv.8-11 with vv.5-7 in one row is not a shared temporal frame but the evaluative verdict vv.6-7 pass on Jehoram -- that he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as Ahab's house did, doing evil in Yahweh's sight -- under which the Edom and Libnah revolts (8-10) and the cultic apostasy (11) accumulate as the substantiating record, one continuous catalog of the evil the verdict names, rather than a catalog Elijah's letter itself recites as a totality: the letter (12-13) charges only failure to walk in Jehoshaphat and Asa's ways, prostituting Judah and Jerusalem like the house of Ahab, and killing brothers -- answering v.4's fratricide, outside this row's own span, not the Edom/Libnah revolts of vv.8-10 by name. Severing at v.8 would still divide the verdict from its own substantiating record; that the catalog's own opening marker is real and tier-1-eligible is conceded, and a split there remains a live, credible alternative this row does not claim to foreclose.

boundary_rationale: The letter inset opens with its own frame, “וַיָּבֹ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מִכְתָּ֔ב מֵֽאֵלִיָּ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא לֵאמֹ֑ר” (“A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying,” WEB 21:12), and its curses name two targets: “הִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה נֹגֵ֛ף מַגֵּפָ֥ה גְדוֹלָ֖ה בְּעַמֶּ֑ךָ” (“Yahweh will strike your people with a great plague,” WEB 21:14) continuing into “וּבְבָנֶ֥יךָ וּבְנָשֶׁ֖יךָ וּבְכָל רְכוּשֶֽׁךָ” (“including your children, your wives, and all your possessions,” WEB 21:14) and the bowel-disease curse of v15. Per the inset rule the letter cannot be isolated as its own row because no closing frame resumes ordinary narration afterward; instead v16 launches directly into the first fulfillment, “וַיַּעֲל֤וּ בִֽיהוּדָה֙ וַיִּבְקָע֔וּהָ וַיִּשְׁבּ֗וּ אֵ֤ת כָּל הָרְכוּשׁ֙ הַנִּמְצָ֣א לְבֵית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ” (“they came up against Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the possessions that were found in the king's house,” WEB 21:17), echoed almost verbally by “וְגַם בָּנָ֖יו וְנָשָׁ֑יו” (“including his sons and his wives,” WEB 21:17) against the curse's own “your children...your wives”. This lexical repetition binds letter and invasion into one unit. The row closes at v17 because v18's “after all this” opens the second, later stage of judgment as an explicitly separate time-frame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 21:12-15 as an isolated inset row cannot stand: no bilateral frame closes it off, since v16's new-subject clause reads as direct fulfillment of the letter's own curses rather than a narrative resumption, so the host unit's integrity requires keeping letter and fulfillment together.

boundary_rationale: An explicit time-frame transition opens this row: וְאַחֲרֵ֖י כָּל זֹ֑את ("After all this," WEB 21:18), a construction distinct from 8:1's own וַיְהִ֞י מִקֵּ֣ץ עֶשְׂרִ֣ים שָׁנָ֗ה (a different, single-instance formula) and matched instead, near-identically, by 35:20's אַחֲרֵ֣י כָל זֹ֗את, which opens the Necho unit; the shared idiom marks both as time-frame transitions, here separating the second curse's fulfillment (incurable bowel disease) from the first (invasion, vv16-17). The row runs through the two-year decline and death (v19) and closes on the reign-closing double formula: the age-and-length notice repeated from v5's own בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וּשְׁתַּ֛יִם שָׁנָ֖ה יְהוֹרָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֑וֹ, with both the year-noun and the king's name giving way to the auxiliary verb הָיָה, בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וּשְׁתַּ֨יִם֙ הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֔וֹ -- an auxiliary-verb-for-name substitution recurring nowhere else in the book except, in a narrower form, at Jotham's own matching closing formula, 27:8's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְחָמֵ֛שׁ שָׁנָ֖ה הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ where only the name gives way to the auxiliary verb while the year-noun is retained, against his named opening at 27:1 -- then וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ בְּלֹ֣א חֶמְדָּ֔ה וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֨הוּ֙ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֔יד וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים ("he departed with no one's regret...they buried him in David's city, but not in the tombs of the kings," WEB 21:20) - a dishonorable-burial notice that also seams Jehoram's whole account out before Ahaziah's accession opens ch.22.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding vv16-17 into this row is unconvincing, since “after all this” at v18 explicitly marks a distinct, later stage of judgment rather than a continuation of the same invasion scene.

boundary_rationale: This reign account opens on an irregular installation formula rather than the usual father-to-son succession clause: וַיַּמְלִיכוּ֩ יוֹשְׁבֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם אֶת אֲחַזְיָ֨הוּ בְנ֤וֹ הַקָּטֹן֙ תַּחְתָּ֔יו כִּ֤י ("The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah his youngest son king in his place...because," WEB 22:1), the causal clause explaining why the people, not custom, chose him (his older brothers slain by the raiders of v1), closed within the same verse by the ordinary qal formula וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲחַזְיָ֥הוּ בֶן יְהוֹרָ֖ם מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה ("Ahaziah...reigned," v.1b) -- an accession notice complete in its own clause-type but irregular in substance, since it reports an installation by the people rather than a straightforward succession. The age formula proper, בֶּן אַרְבָּעִ֨ים וּשְׁתַּ֤יִם שָׁנָה֙ אֲחַזְיָ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֔וֹ (v.2), is the same device-type that opens a fresh reign-account on its own at 21:5 within this very part, and pmarks keys a PE (single-witness) to the very 22:1/22:2 juncture; both are disclosed here rather than treated as absent. What keeps v.2 inside this row rather than launching its own is that v.1's own accession is already anomalous -- an installation explained by a causal clause about slain brothers, not the book's standard succession pattern -- so v.2's age notice completes the standard accession-and-evaluation report v.1 alone leaves irregular, rather than opening independent material the way the identical formula does at 21:5. The actual ground distinguishing the two loci is not narrative closure -- 21:20 closes Jehoram's account in full immediately before 22:1, exactly as 21:1 closes Jehoshaphat's before 21:2, and in both cases new-king narrative then intervenes before the age formula (three verses at 21:2-4 versus one at 22:1) -- but v.1's own installation clause, which names its agents (the inhabitants of Jerusalem) and supplies a causal clause explaining the irregular choice (his older brothers slain by raiders), with no counterpart at 21:1's own bare death-burial-succession formula. The row carries through the war at Ramoth Gilead, Jehu's purge, and Ahaziah's death, closing on the explicit dynasty-collapse clause וְאֵין֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ לַעְצֹ֥ר כֹּ֖חַ לְמַמְלָכָֽה ("The house of Ahaziah had no power to hold the kingdom," WEB 22:9) - a summary formula terminating this reign before Athaliah's countercoup opens at v10 with a fresh, fronted subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 22:2, treating v.1 alone as the accession notice and vv.2-9 as the reign-and-collapse account, is the stronger rival -- not the v.6/v.7 seam this row previously leaned on, where v.7 merely interprets the immediately preceding wound as divine causation rather than opening independent material. The 22:1/22:2 split is nonetheless not adopted here because v.1's own installation clause remains anomalous until v.2's age notice completes it; the reader should weigh for themselves whether that completion-relationship outweighs the identical age-formula device opening a fresh unit seventeen verses earlier, at 21:5 (sixteen verses intervening, since chapter 21 runs the full twenty verses before 22:1 opens).

boundary_rationale: A fronted new subject opens the row: “וַעֲתַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֵ֣ם אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ רָאֲתָ֖ה כִּ֣י מֵ֣ת בְּנָ֑הּ וַתָּ֗קָם” (“Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose,” WEB 22:10), pivoting away from Ahaziah's own reign account just closed by v9's dynasty-collapse formula. The rescue of Joash by Jehoshabeath (v11) is the direct counter-action, and the row closes on the interval-summary clause “וַיְהִ֤י אִתָּם֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים מִתְחַבֵּ֖א שֵׁ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וַעֲתַלְיָ֖ה מֹלֶ֥כֶת עַל הָאָֽרֶץ” (“he was with them hidden in God's house six years while Athaliah reigned over the land,” WEB 22:12), which compresses the whole six-year span into a single retrospective notice - a natural resting point before 23:1's fresh “in the seventh year” marker resumes the story. A pe stands after 22:12 in WLC's sole witness, offering its usual weak support. This close is nonetheless the more contested edge of the wider Athaliah arc (22:10-23:21): the six-year summary is a narrative pause, not necessarily a hard terminus, though it is the only edge in this three-verse stretch that names a completed span of time.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 22:10-23:21 as one undivided decision is a live alternative, since v.12's interval-summary supplies its own internal closure even though both halves remain bracketed by the larger usurpation-to-overthrow arc; that closure is a narrative pause, not necessarily a hard terminus, and the split here does not depend on any project pacing target to be justified.

boundary_rationale: Opening edge: וּבַשָּׁנָ֨ה הַשְּׁבִעִ֜ית הִתְחַזַּ֣ק יְהוֹיָדָ֗ע וַיִּקַּ֣ח ("In the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took," WEB 23:1) supplies a fresh temporal anchor, a tier-1 time-frame transition, and a new agent taking initiative. The hitpael-חזק verb itself is not a marked echo of Jehoram's own power-seizure at 21:4 (וַיִּתְחַזַּ֔ק): the stem recurs eleven times as a finite verb across the whole book plus two infinitives inside speeches, several of them mid-account rather than at any unit's opening (וַיִּתְחַזֵּ֣ק at 13:21, after Abijah's war; הִתְחַזַּ֔ק at 25:11, inside Amaziah's Edom campaign; וַיִּתְחַזַּ֡ק at 32:5, inside Hezekiah's defensive works) -- the Chronicler's ordinary consolidation idiom, not a bespoke signal tying this seam to 21:4's. The seam itself rests on the fronted temporal phrase alone. The row carries the covenant with the captains, the gathering of Levites, Jehoiada's deployment speech (vv3-7, kept inside this host unit since v8's “so the Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada...commanded” is a command-fulfillment pairing, not an isolating frame), and the execution of the plan through the acclamation “וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ יְחִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ” (“they said, ‘Long live the king!’,” WEB 23:11), corroborated weakly by the samekh at 23:11 (single-witness, Writings). The seventh-year marker that opens this row is nonetheless the more debatable edge of the wider arc: WEB 22:12's six-year interval notice does not read as an unambiguous terminus, so 23:1's opening could equally be read as mere continuation within one unbroken Athaliah narrative rather than a fresh unit-opener.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this row with 22:10-12 into a single continuous Athaliah-arc decision is a live alternative, since the interval clause at 22:12 is not a hard narrative terminus and “in the seventh year” could function as pure continuation; the split is kept here because the fronted temporal transition alone -- not the hitpael-חזק verb, which is the book's ordinary consolidation idiom -- marks a new initiating moment, but the case is not decisive either way.

boundary_rationale: A clean subject shift opens the row, from the crowd's celebration to Athaliah's perception of it: “וַתִּשְׁמַ֣ע עֲתַלְיָ֗הוּ” (“Athaliah heard,” WEB 23:12), a pivot corroborated weakly by the SAMEKH mark keyed to 23:11 (single-witness), immediately behind this seam rather than inside it, leading into her cry וַתֹּ֖אמֶר קֶ֥שֶׁר קָֽשֶׁר ("Treason! treason!," WEB 23:13). A second SAMEKH keyed to 23:13 falls interior to this span, at the 13/14 seam between the cry and Jehoiada's counter-order, and is disclosed here as non-driving color rather than boundary evidence. Jehoiada's counter-order (v14) and her removal follow, and the scene closes flatly on “וַיְמִית֖וּהָ שָֽׁם” (“they killed her there,” WEB 23:15) - a terse notice, its sole-witness pe adding the same weak confirmation, that ends the episode before v16 opens an entirely different ceremonial register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the prior row through the coronation to include this scene undersells the seam, since “Athaliah heard” at v12 is a clear pivot to her perspective, distinct from the priestly execution of Jehoiada's plan that precedes it.

boundary_rationale: A fresh covenant ceremony opens the row, distinct in scope from the covenants that preceded it: “וַיִּכְרֹ֤ת יְהוֹיָדָע֙ בְּרִ֔ית בֵּינ֕וֹ” (“Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king,” WEB 23:16), now binding the nation itself to be Yahweh's people, rather than the captains' covenant of v.1 and the assembly's dynastic pact of v.3. The distinction rests on 23:16's own purpose clause -- “to be a people to Yahweh” -- with no counterpart at v.1 or v.3, and on the change of covenanting agent: Jehoiada personally at v.16, rather than the whole assembly at v.3, whose party otherwise overlaps v.16's almost entirely. The Baal-house demolition and priestly restoration follow; v.20's procession then moves the young king bodily out of the temple and installs him on the throne, וַיּ֤וֹרֶד אֶת הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מִבֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה...וַיּוֹשִׁ֨יבוּ֙ אֶת הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֥א הַמַּמְלָכָֽה ("...brought the king down from Yahweh's house. They came...and set the king on the throne of the kingdom," v.20), a genuine location-and-participant change of the class this book elsewhere treats as boundary-driving, and the strongest internal rival in this span; it is kept inside this row because the enthronement is the covenant's own completion, not a separate topic -- the throne-installation is what makes the people's earlier acclamation of the king (v.11) institutionally real, continuous with the purge and restoration rather than a fresh initiative. The row closes on וַיִּשְׂמְח֥וּ כָל עַם הָאָ֖רֶץ וְהָעִ֣יר שָׁקָ֑טָה וְאֶת עֲתַלְיָ֖הוּ הֵמִ֥יתוּ בֶחָֽרֶב ("all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They had slain Athaliah with the sword," WEB 23:21); WLC's sole witness appends a samekh right here too, for whatever that weak testimony is worth. This recap clause also answers 22:10 as a motif of violence recoiling on its author, rather than a formal inclusio: Athaliah seized power over the royal line by violence, וַעֲתַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֵ֣ם אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ רָאֲתָ֖ה כִּ֣י מֵ֣ת בְּנָ֑הּ וַתָּ֗קָם וַתְּדַבֵּ֛ר אֶת כָּל זֶ֥רַע הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה לְבֵ֥ית יְהוּדָֽה ("Athaliah...saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal offspring of the house of Judah," WEB 22:10), and here falls to violence in turn; the two verses share only the מות root, not a repeated phrase, so the frame is thematic -- violence recoiling on its author -- rather than a true bracket, and this row itself is bounded on its own terms by the covenant-renewal formula that opens it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.20 to separate the Baal-purge-and-restoration report (16-19) from the enthronement procession (20-21) is the stronger internal rival, since v.20 supplies a genuine change of location and cast; it is not adopted because the throne-installation completes rather than launches the same covenant-restoration movement begun at v.16, and 22:10-23:21 remains bracketed as one violence-answers-violence arc regardless of where the internal seam falls.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the standard age formula “בֶּן שֶׁ֤בַע שָׁנִים֙ יֹאָ֣שׁ בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְאַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ צִבְיָ֖ה מִבְּאֵ֥ר שָֽׁבַע” (“Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem,” WEB 24.1), followed at once by the evaluative clause naming the mentorship frame: “כָּל יְמֵ֖י יְהוֹיָדָ֥ע הַכֹּהֵֽן” (“all the days of Jehoiada the priest,” WEB 24:2). The same phrase recurs to close the unit at v14, shorn of its appositional title and with an added adverb, תָּמִ֔יד כֹּ֖ל יְמֵ֥י יְהוֹיָדָֽע ("continually all the days of Jehoiada," WEB 24:14) -- v14 drops הַכֹּהֵֽן and adds תָּמִ֔יד, so the bracket is a lexical echo rather than a byte-identical repetition, forming a loose inclusio around the mentored era. Inside that bracket, וַיְהִ֖י אַחֲרֵי כֵ֑ן ("After this," WEB 24:4) opens the repair project's own narrative (intent, fundraising, the chest, the workmen, completion and vessels); this construction is tier-1-eligible in its own right -- the same vayehi-plus-acharei-ken collocation occurs exactly once more in the book, at 20:1, where it alone opens a fresh unit (M8-2Chr-076) rather than being absorbed into anything preceding it -- so the inclusio does not by itself neutralize v.4 as a candidate seam the way this row's whole case requires. What keeps this row unsplit, honestly, is weaker than the inclusio alone suggests: the repair sequence's register-like, procedural character ("thus they did day by day," v11) parallels the coarser treatment construction catalogs receive elsewhere in the book -- specifically the book strategy's own instruction to keep chapters 3-4's construction material coarse (book_strategy_draft.md §5) -- and the mentored-era bracket still supplies a real, if lexical rather than verbatim, frame around the whole. But v.4's own vayehi-acharei-ken construction ties it to the 20:1 parallel, a live, tier-1-class rival this argument does not defeat. The row closes precisely where the inclusio phrase closes; a pe stands there too in the sole surviving witness, weak and corroborative only.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v4 to separate the accession/evaluation notice from the repair-project narrative deserves real weight, not a quick dismissal: v.4's vayehi-acharei-ken construction is the same tier-1 time-frame-transition device that alone opens M8-2Chr-076 at 20:1, and an inclusio does not automatically outrank a tier-1 opener standing inside it. The row is kept whole here on the weaker ground that the mentored-era bracket (vv2/14) and the repair project's own coarse, catalog-like register still read as one accountable unit, but this defense does not defeat the 20:1 parallel, which remains a live rival.

boundary_rationale: A short, self-contained obituary opens this row the moment the repair-project inclusio closes: “וַיִּזְקַ֧ן יְהוֹיָדָ֛ע וַיִּשְׂבַּ֥ע יָמִ֖ים וַיָּמֹ֑ת בֶּן מֵאָ֧ה וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֛ים שָׁנָ֖ה בְּמוֹתֽוֹ” (“Jehoiada grew old and was full of days, and he died; he was one hundred thirty years old when he died,” WEB 24:15). It closes on the honorable-burial rationale, extending to the verse's own terminus, “...among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house,” WEB 24:16; the lone witness sets a SAMEKH after the verse's own final word, for what little that is worth. The contrast is with dishonor, not mere formula-repetition: Jehoram's burial closes “וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים” (“not in the tombs of the kings,” 21:20), and Joash's own reign later closes “וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים” (“they didn’t bury him in the tombs of the kings,” 24:25) — the same denial, expanded with a resumptive verb (קְבָרֻ֖הוּ) Jehoiada's own notice is spared. Brevity here reflects the notice's hinge function: it is the pivot between “all the days of Jehoiada” (v2/v14) and “after the death of Jehoiada” (v17), not a continuation of either surrounding unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this notice into the following apostasy account does not work, since v17's “after the death of Jehoiada” is itself an opening time-marker for the next unit, presupposing rather than continuing this obituary.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the deliberate antithesis of the just-closed inclusio phrase: “וְאַֽחֲרֵ֥י מוֹת֙ יְה֣וֹיָדָ֔ע” (“Now after the death of Jehoiada,” WEB 24:17), signaling the reversal of everything held while he lived. Prophets are sent and rejected (vv18-19), then Zechariah's Spirit-empowered indictment opens with its own frame, “וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֖ד מֵעַ֣ל לָעָ֑ם וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים” (“he stood above the people, and said to them, ‘God says,’” WEB 24:20); per the inset rule this oracle stays inside the host apostasy account because v21's stoning is an immediate narrative reaction, not a resumption after a gap. The row closes on Zechariah's dying imprecation “וּכְמוֹת֣וֹ אָמַ֔ר יֵ֥רֶא יְהוָ֖ה וְיִדְרֹֽשׁ” (“he said, ‘May Yahweh look at it, and repay it,’” WEB 24:22) - the single witness appends a pe here too, weak as always - a curse that v23's time-marker answers directly in the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating Zechariah's oracle (24:20) as its own row overreaches: no resumption formula separates it from the stoning that immediately follows, so the speech must stay inside its host unit per the inset rule.

boundary_rationale: A PE (single-witness) stands at 24:22, weak corroboration for the opening edge. Opens on the time-marker that directly answers Zechariah's dying curse: “וַיְהִ֣י לִתְקוּפַ֣ת הַשָּׁנָ֗ה עָלָ֣ה עָלָיו֮ חֵ֣יל אֲרָם֒” (“At the end of the year, the army of the Syrians came up against him,” WEB 24:23), followed by the explicit theological framing of v24 (“a small company...because they had forsaken Yahweh”). The conspirators' motive is stated in kind: “הִתְקַשְּׁר֨וּ עָלָ֜יו עֲבָדָ֗יו בִּדְמֵי֙ בְּנֵי֙ יְהוֹיָדָ֣ע הַכֹּהֵ֔ן” (“his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest,” WEB 24:25). A SAMEKH (single-witness, weak) follows v.25, interior to this row's own span; it does not disturb the absorption of vv.26-27 into this unit. 24:25's dishonor-notice differs from 21:20's by exactly one inserted word: 21:20 simply denies burial “וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים”, while 24:25 repeats that same denial with a resumptive verb wedged in, “וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים”, a form (קְבָרֻ֖הוּ) attested nowhere else in this book. V26 then names the conspirators, “וְאֵ֖לֶּה הַמִּתְקַשְּׁרִ֣ים עָלָ֑יו זָבָ֗ד בֶּן שִׁמְעָת֙ הָֽעַמּוֹנִ֔ית וִיה֣וֹזָבָ֔ד בֶּן שִׁמְרִ֖ית הַמּוֹאָבִֽית”; this ve'eleh-plus-demonstrative opener does head a list-register elsewhere in the book (foundation measurements at 3:3, the chief-officer register at 8:10, the fathers'-house muster at 17:14), and its demonstrative here is cataphoric in exactly the same way -- pointing forward to the two names, Zabad and Jehozabad, that follow it, not backward to the assassination just narrated. What ties v.26 to v.25 instead is the pronominal suffix and the participle: the suffix takes Joash, killed in v.25, as its antecedent, and the participle echoes v.25's own finite verb of conspiring -- v.26 supplies the killers' identity for a death already reported through this suffix-and-participle echo, not through its own opening demonstrative, and nothing resumes or reopens the narrative after it before v27's citation. The row closes on the fixed pair that ends nearly every reign account in the book: the source-citation formula “הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל מִדְרַ֖שׁ סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֑ים” (“behold, they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings,” WEB 24:27) and the succession clause “וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Amaziah his son reigned in his place,” WEB 24:27); a final PE in the sole witness closes the paragraph here as well - the seam-out point into the next part's Amaziah accession.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off v26 alone as its own register-opening unit fails, not because its own demonstrative is anaphoric -- it is cataphoric, like the book's other list-openers -- but because v.26 depends on v.25 through the suffix-and-participle echo that ties the killers' identity to the assassination just narrated, so it does not stand free the way a genuine list-opener would; splitting vv26-27 together from the invasion/death narrative would still sever the fixed source-citation-and-succession pair from the reign it closes.

boundary_rationale: The reign opens on the fixed age-formula, “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ מָלַ֣ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים וָתֵ֨שַׁע֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ יְהוֹעַדָּ֖ן מִירוּשָׁלָֽיִם” (“Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign” WEB), pairing accession age, reign-length, and mother's name in the same formulaic slot the book fills again for his son and grandson later in this very part. It is immediately followed, still inside the same reporting frame, by the evaluation clause “וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה רַ֕ק לֹ֖א בְּלֵבָ֥ב שָׁלֵֽם”, whose reservation (WEB: “but not with a perfect heart”) already signals a qualified reign. The unit closes because v3 pivots into a narrated circumstantial clause rather than continuing the formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through the purge of the assassins (to v4) would merge a closed formulaic report with a freshly-opened narrative episode that has its own grammatical opener.

boundary_rationale: A circumstantial clause launches this episode: “וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר חָזְקָ֥ה הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה עָלָ֑יו וַֽיַּהֲרֹג֙ אֶת עֲבָדָ֔יו הַמַּכִּ֖ים אֶת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָבִֽיו” (“when the kingdom was established to him, he killed his servants who had killed his father the king”). Verse-initial wayehi opens 38 verses across 2Chr, a common general device for launching narrative material, but this exact collocation — וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר plus חָזְקָ֥ה הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה — occurs nowhere else in the book; the seam rests on a book-wide singleton use of a common opener-type, which if anything sharpens rather than weakens the edge, since the specific wording marks this precise juncture rather than reusing a stock formula. The episode narrates the killing of his father's assassins and then anchors its restraint in an explicit legal citation, “כִּ֣י כַכָּת֣וּב בַּתּוֹרָ֡ה בְּסֵ֣פֶר מֹשֶׁה֩ אֲשֶׁר צִוָּ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה לֵאמֹ֗ר” (“according to that which is written in the law, in the book of Moses”), closing on the quoted maxim. A PE space-mark follows v4 (single-witness, weak corroboration only); v5 then turns to military mobilization, a topic change from justice to muster, though the grammatical subject remains the same: Amaziah continues as the 3ms actor across vv.3-5, renominalised at v.5's own opening verb rather than introduced as a fresh subject. The row's own close accordingly rests on the closed legal-citation terminus at v.4's end and the topic shift itself, corroborated by the single-witness PE already cited after v.4, not on any change of grammatical subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading vv3-4 as still part of the accession report (1-4 combined) would collapse the closed evaluation formula into an open narrative episode that only begins with its own circumstantial clause.

boundary_rationale: Amaziah's own mobilization opens the row: “וַיִּקְבֹּ֤ץ אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֶת יְהוּדָ֔ה” (“Amaziah gathered Judah together”) — an unmarked wayyiqtol carrying Amaziah forward as the same grammatical subject from the purge just closed, not the locational motion-verb device the book uses to mark a genuine scene change (“וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ רְחַבְעָ֖ם שְׁכֶ֑מָה”, 10:1) nor the subject-fronted disjunctive this same reign uses six verses later (“וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק”, v11); the seam here rests on topic-shift (justice to muster) as its only tier-1 signal, a weaker warrant than the row's own neighbors supply, which the medium grade already registers; a PE (single-witness) follows 25:4 immediately before this seam, weak tier-3 corroboration only, not counted among the tier-1 signals just described. It runs through the mercenary hire in v6, “וַיִּשְׂכֹּ֣ר מִיִּשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵ֥אָה אֶ֛לֶף גִּבּ֥וֹר חָ֖יִל בְּמֵאָ֥ה כִכַּר כָּֽסֶף” (“he hired one hundred thousand mighty men of valor out of Israel for one hundred talents of silver”); that hundred-talent absolute (בְּמֵאָ֥ה כִכַּר) is the hook Amaziah himself, not the man of God, reopens at v9 — “וּמַֽה לַּעֲשׂוֹת֙ לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִגְד֣וּד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל” (“what shall we do for the hundred talents which I have given to the army of Israel?”), with the construct לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר answering back to v6's absolute; the man of God's own words in vv7-8 never mention money at all. The row closes because v7 introduces the man of God with the entry formula “וְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הַמֶּ֕לֶךְ אַל יָבֹ֥א עִמְּךָ֖ צְבָ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כֹּ֖ל בְּנֵ֥י אֶפְרָֽיִם”.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging vv5-6 with the preceding purge narrative (3-6 as one unit) remains a live rival precisely because v5's seam is topic-shift alone, without the locational or disjunctive marking that isolates other scene-changes in this reign (10:1, 25:11); the medium grade reflects that the row is kept separate on topic alone, not on a stronger grammatical signal.

boundary_rationale: Framed by the entry formula “וְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הַמֶּ֕לֶךְ אַל יָבֹ֥א עִמְּךָ֖ צְבָ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כֹּ֖ל בְּנֵ֥י אֶפְרָֽיִם” (“A man of God came to him, saying”), an unnamed prophet's warning against hiring Israelite troops opens as a clearly bounded speech unit. It runs through the exchange in v9, closing on his reply “וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ לְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים וּמַֽה לַּעֲשׂוֹת֙ לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִגְד֣וּד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים יֵ֚שׁ לַֽיהוָ֔ה לָ֥תֶת לְךָ֖ הַרְבֵּ֥ה מִזֶּֽה” (“Yahweh is able to give you much more than this”). The host narrative resumes immediately after in v10 with Amaziah again as grammatical subject of a plain wayyiqtol, “וַיַּבְדִּילֵ֣ם אֲמַצְיָ֗הוּ” (“Then Amaziah separated them”), satisfying the inset rule's requirement of a tier-1 frame on both sides.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv7-10 as one continuous mobilization scene would erase the direct-speech frame that isolates the oracle and would leave the muster report (5-6) without any narrative close of its own.

boundary_rationale: This stretch gathers three closely-linked beats around a single grievance: the dismissal notice in v10, “וַיַּבְדִּילֵ֣ם אֲמַצְיָ֗הוּ לְהַגְּדוּד֙ אֲשֶׁר בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מֵֽאֶפְרַ֔יִם לָלֶ֖כֶת לִמְקוֹמָ֑ם וַיִּ֨חַר אַפָּ֤ם מְאֹד֙ בִּֽיהוּדָ֔ה וַיָּשׁ֥וּבוּ לִמְקוֹמָ֖ם בָּחֳרִי אָֽף”, ends on the Ephraimites' anger; a disjunctive subject-first clause then pivots to Amaziah's own resolve, “וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק” (“Amaziah took courage”), launching the Edom campaign; and v13 explicitly recalls the dismissed troop by name, “וּבְנֵ֣י הַגְּד֗וּד אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵשִׁ֤יב אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מִלֶּ֤כֶת עִמּוֹ֙ לַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה” (“the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back”), showing the raid on Judah's cities is the direct payoff of v10's dismissal. The Masoretic tradition marks this stretch at three points: a PE follows v.10, a SAMEKH follows v.12 (both interior to the span), and a SAMEKH follows v.13 -- all single-witness, weak corroboration only. V14's temporal clause opens an unrelated topic.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The harder rival is not merely lifting v10 out, but stopping the unit there and letting vv11-13 stand as their own row on the strength of v11's disjunctive, “וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק”, which does break the wayyiqtol chain v10 sustains; that disjunctive, though, marks a shift of narrative attention back onto Amaziah after the aside about the dismissed troops' anger, not a change of scene, time, or addressee, and v13's anaphoric recall of that same dismissed troop shows the dismissal, the campaign, and the raid are one grievance-driven sequence rather than two.

boundary_rationale: A fresh scene begins where the campaign notice left off: “וַיְהִ֗י אַחֲרֵ֨י ב֤וֹא אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֵֽהַכּ֣וֹת אֶת אֲדוֹמִ֔ים” (“after Amaziah had come from the slaughter of the Edomites”), the same class of temporal-transition device the book uses at other major scene changes. The row's own internal candidate is v15's anger-plus-dispatch formula, “וַיִּֽחַר אַ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה בַּאֲמַצְיָ֑הוּ וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֵלָיו֙ נָבִ֔יא וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ” (“Yahweh's anger burned against Amaziah, and he sent to him a prophet who said to him”), which shares its messenger-plus-speech-introduction shape with the book's other prophet-notice frames (Hanani's “וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא בָּ֚א חֲנָ֣נִי הָרֹאֶ֔ה אֶל אָסָ֖א”, 16:7-9). Unlike Hanani's notice, which opens after an already-completed and separately-narrated war episode, v15's anger clause is the direct, grammatically-marked consequence of the idolatry just narrated in v14 (the gods of the children of Seir he had just set up) -- nothing but the anger clause itself stands between sin and rebuke, so splitting v14 from v15-16 would sever a single cause-and-response unit at its own hinge rather than at an independent scene-opening frame. Amaziah's adoption of Seir's gods draws that prophet's rebuke, which the king cuts off mid-speech (v16); the row closes on the prophet's own last word, “כִּֽי עָשִׂ֣יתָ זֹּ֔את וְלֹ֥א שָׁמַ֖עְתָּ לַעֲצָתִֽי” (“because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel”), a direct-speech terminus. A PE space-marker in the Masoretic tradition sits after v16 too (single-witness, corroborative weight only); v17 then opens an entirely new diplomatic scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The closer rival -- splitting v14's idolatry notice from vv15-16's prophetic rebuke at the anger-plus-dispatch formula -- fails because that formula is the marked, grammatically-signaled consequence of v14's sin, not an independent scene-opening frame, so the cut would sever one cause-and-response unit at its own hinge. Extending this row through vv17-19 instead would fail for a different reason: v.17 renominalizes the subject and turns to a new addressee, Joash of Israel, opening a distinct diplomatic scene.

boundary_rationale: Diplomatic correspondence opens the row with a messenger formula, “וַיִּוָּעַ֗ץ אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה וַ֠יִּשְׁלַח” (“Amaziah...consulted...and sent to Joash”), matching the class of scene/participant-change device the book uses to launch new episodes. Joash's reply is a taunting fable, opening “הַח֜וֹחַ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּלְּבָנ֗וֹן שָׁ֠לַח אֶל הָאֶ֜רֶז אֲשֶׁ֤ר בַּלְּבָנוֹן֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תְּנָֽה” (“The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar”), and it closes on the fable's moral in direct speech, “וְנָ֣פַלְתָּ֔ אַתָּ֖ה וִיהוּדָ֥ה עִמָּֽךְ” (“you should fall, even you and Judah with you”). The row ends there because v20 shifts from quoted dialogue to the narrator's own theological verdict.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the exchange straight through the battle (17-24 as one unit) would flatten the clean pivot from quoted taunt-speech to narrated military outcome that v20 itself marks.

boundary_rationale: v20's own clause is retrospective comment rather than a fresh opener: “וְלֹא שָׁמַ֣ע אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ כִּ֤י מֵהָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ הִ֔יא” (“Amaziah would not listen; for it was of God”) reaches backward, its causal clause “כִּ֣י דָֽרְשׁ֔וּ אֵ֖ת אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֱדֽוֹם” (“because they had sought after the gods of Edom”) answering the prophet's own charge at v15, “לָ֤מָּה דָרַ֨שְׁתָּ֙ אֶת אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם” (“why have you sought after the gods of the people”), and its bare pronoun הִ֔יא finding no antecedent inside the verse itself. The same waw-negative-qatal-plus-divine-causation shape closes the Rehoboam standoff at 10:15, “וְלֹֽא שָׁמַ֥ע הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶל הָעָ֑ם כִּֽי הָיְתָ֤ה נְסִבָּה֙ מֵעִ֣ם הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים” (“the king didn't listen to the people; for it was brought about by God”), which likewise looks back at the just-finished exchange rather than opening the section that follows at 10:16 — the parallel is instructive: in both places the clause functions as the narrator's own verdict-hinge that turns a quoted confrontation into narrated consequence, not as a formulaic unit-opener in its own right. What licenses grouping v.20 forward with vv.21-24 here, unlike 10:15's own backward-looking placement relative to 10:16, is what follows each verdict-hinge: 10:16's sequel is the people's own quoted response, a new speech-act rather than a narrated consequence, so 10:15 closes the exchange it comments on; 25:21's sequel instead narrates the very consequence 25:20's verdict predicts -- Joash's advance and the ensuing battle -- so 25:20 opens the sequence it explains rather than closing the one before it. That is why this row keeps vv20-24 together as the single divine-judgment sequence the verdict frames — defeat at Beth Shemesh, capture, the breach of Jerusalem's wall, and the plunder of the temple and palace — rather than opening at v21's own re-nominated “וַיַּ֨עַל יוֹאָ֤שׁ מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙”, which is a genuine internal rival for a fresh start but would orphan the verdict from the events it explains. It closes on the return notice, “וַיָּ֖שָׁב שֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (gloss: “returned to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition likewise inserts a PE right after v24 (single-witness, merely corroborative). V25 then opens with a verb-initial apocopated wayyiqtol carrying its subject after it, “וַיְחִ֨י אֲמַצְיָ֤הוּ” (“Amaziah…lived”), pivoting the topic to lifespan reckoning rather than fronting any subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger rival is not the wider 17-24 merge but opening at v21's own re-nominated wayyiqtol instead of v20's causal verdict; keeping v20 with vv21-24 is preferred because it is the verse that supplies the divine rationale for the defeat that follows, and severing it would leave that rationale stranded with the taunt-exchange it does not belong to.

boundary_rationale: A verb-initial apocopated wayyiqtol, its subject postposed rather than fronted, opens the close of the reign, “וַיְחִ֨י אֲמַצְיָ֤הוּ בֶן יוֹאָשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה אַחֲרֵ֣י מ֔וֹת יוֹאָ֥שׁ בֶּן יְהוֹאָחָ֖ז מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה”, followed by the standard chronicle formula “וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הֲלֹא֙ הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (“the rest of the acts of Amaziah...written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel”) — the book's regular formula-then-death order, not an exception to it: the identical citation-before-death sequence recurs at Solomon's own close (“וּשְׁאָר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרוֹנִ֑ים” at 9:29, followed by 9:30's reign total, “וַיִּמְלֹ֨ךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֧ה בִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה”, then death at 9:31) and at Abijah's (13:22, then web 14:1/MT 13:23); two loci reverse this order rather than one: Josiah's close (35:26), following a death already narrated, and Joash's own earlier close within this book (24:25-27), where death and burial are narrated first at 24:25, וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים (“they buried him in David's city, but they didn't bury him in the tombs of the kings,” WEB 24:25), with the citation-plus-succession formula following only at 24:27, וִיסוֹד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל מִדְרַ֖שׁ סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֑ים וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו (“they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings...Amaziah his son reigned in his place,” WEB 24:27). A further non-conforming case, 36:8, gives the citation-and-succession formula together with no death or burial notice for Jehoiakim anywhere in the book, וְהַנִּמְצָ֣א עָלָ֔יו הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל סֵ֛פֶר מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹיָכִ֥ין בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו (“they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah...Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place,” WEB 36:8). The conspiracy notice then opens with its own temporal clause, “וּמֵעֵ֗ת אֲשֶׁר סָ֤ר אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֵאַחֲרֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיִּקְשְׁר֨וּ עָלָ֥יו קֶ֛שֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם” (“from the time that Amaziah turned away from following Yahweh, they made a conspiracy”), and the unit closes the chapter with burial. 26:1's fresh accession notice, “all the people of Judah took Uzziah,” marks the seam-out.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the source-citation formula (v26) from the conspiracy-and-death notice (27-28) would isolate a single closing clause from the reign-summary complex it functions inside, against the formula's usual role elsewhere in the book as a unit-closer paired with what follows it.

boundary_rationale: Uzziah's enthronement is narrated by the people rather than by the standard age-formula: “וַיִּקְח֞וּ כָּל עַ֤ם יְהוּדָה֙ אֶת עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ” (“All the people of Judah took Uzziah...and made him king”), a distinct accession-type from the age-formula used for his father and son (25:1's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ מָלַ֣ךְ and 27:1's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יוֹתָ֣ם) -- and a genuine structural twin of its own kind recurs at 36:1, “וַיִּקְחוּ֙ עַם הָאָ֔רֶץ אֶת” (“the people of the land took Jehoahaz”), narrowed to the take-and-install verb pairing 26:1 itself uses, this is the only other place in the book where 'the people' take and then install a king -- two further installations by 'the people' exist without a preceding take-verb, at 22:1 (וַיַּמְלִיכוּ֩ יוֹשְׁבֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם, “the inhabitants of Jerusalem made...king”) and 33:25 (וַיַּמְלִ֧יכוּ עַם הָאָ֛רֶץ, “the people of the land made...king”), and 33:25's own phrase is verbally closer to 36:1's identical phrasing than to 26:1's own 'all the people of Judah'. V2 appends a building note and a retrospective death-notice for Amaziah, closing on “אַחֲרֵ֥י שְׁכַֽב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ עִם אֲבֹתָֽיו” (“after that the king slept with his fathers”) — the king in question being Amaziah, not Uzziah, a clause that looks backward rather than forward. Masoretic spacing marks the same spot with a PE after v2 (single-witness only), and v3 then restarts with the standard age-formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging vv1-2 straight into the formal age-formula (1-5 as one unit) would paper over the fact that the book gives Uzziah two distinct accession notices in immediate succession, a doubling worth isolating rather than smoothing over.

boundary_rationale: Only after the popular acclamation does the book supply the standard accession formula, “בֶּן שֵׁ֨שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ עֻזִּיָּ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֔וֹ וַחֲמִשִּׁ֤ים וּשְׁתַּ֨יִם֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם” (“Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign”), restating the age datum already given at v1 (“וְה֕וּא בֶּן שֵׁ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָ֑ה”, which carries no reign-length figure at all) — a genuine doublet for age alone, the fifty-two-year reign-length being new information here, whose cause the text does not explain. The evaluation clause “וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂ֖ה אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ אָבִֽיו” follows, and the unit extends through the added piety notice naming Zechariah, closing on “as long as he sought Yahweh, God made him prosper.” The Masoretic tradition places a SAMEKH after v5 too (single-witness, weak corroboration); v6 then opens the military campaign with a bare wayyiqtol chain, “וַיֵּצֵא֙ וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם”, carrying no expressed subject at all — Uzziah is retrieved across a subject switch from the divine name that closes v5, not handed a fresh nominal subject of his own, so the junction is carried by topic and participant focus rather than by any new subject-verb pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv3-5 as continuous with vv1-2 risks obscuring the tier-1 seam where the formulaic register restarts after the narrated popular-enthronement notice has already closed.

boundary_rationale: Military success dominates this stretch, opened by a fresh verb pair with no subject repeated from the pious notice just closed: “וַיֵּצֵא֙ וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים” (“he went out and fought against the Philistines”). Campaigns against Philistia, the Arabians, and Ammonite tribute culminate in a fame-and-strength notice that does not stop at the fame clause alone: “וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ שְׁמוֹ֙ עַד לְב֣וֹא מִצְרַ֔יִם כִּ֥י הֶחֱזִ֖יק עַד לְמָֽעְלָה” (“his name spread abroad even to the entrance of Egypt, for he grew exceedingly strong”) — a hiphil of the same ḥ-z-q root that threads 26:8, 9, 15, and 16 into the hubris pivot two rows later. V9 then opens an unrelated building topic with its own subject-verb pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the building projects of vv9-10 into this row would blend a discrete military-and-fame report with the separate architectural and agricultural catalog that follows.

boundary_rationale: Building, agriculture, and army organization are gathered as one register-like catalog, opening “וַיִּ֨בֶן עֻזִּיָּ֤הוּ מִגְדָּלִים֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם” (“Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem”) and running through towers, cisterns, farmers, a numbered muster, equipment, and siege devices. A SAMEKH sits after v10 (single-witness, weak corroboration only), right at the seam between the building material (vv9-10) and v11's own muster-and-army notice, “וַיְהִ֣י לְעֻזִּיָּ֡הוּ חַיִל֩ עֹשֵׂ֨ה מִלְחָמָ֜ה” (“Uzziah had an army of fighting men”) — a wayehi-plus-lamed-plus-royal-name opener that recurs at 9:25 (“וַיְהִ֨י לִשְׁלֹמֹ֜ה”, Solomon's stalls), 14:7 MT/14:8 WEB (“וַיְהִ֣י לְאָסָ֗א”, Asa's army), 18:1 (“וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט”, Jehoshaphat's wealth), and 32:27 (“וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ”, Hezekiah's treasuries), though none of these four opens a fresh reign-section on its own: 9:25 follows directly on the tribute register of 9:23-24; MT 14:5-7 itself runs the identical fortified-cities-then-walls-and-towers-then-army buildup sequence this row attributes to 26:9-11, so the device recurs mid-sequence there too; and 18:1 and 32:27 both follow other narrative material already underway (the marriage-alliance context and the illness-and-humbling notice of 32:24-26, respectively), not a reign's opening beat. Like its four comparanda, v.11 does not open a new section here either: it continues the same buildup-of-resources theme v9-10 already narrate (fortification capacity, then military capacity), with no temporal or locational marker of the kind that elsewhere marks this book's actual scene changes (the temporal-transition opener at 8:1, וַיְהִ֞י מִקֵּ֣ץ עֶשְׂרִ֣ים שָׁנָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּנָ֧ה שְׁלֹמֹ֛ה אֶת בֵּ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה וְאֶת בֵּיתֽוֹ; the motion-verb-plus-place opener at 10:1, וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ רְחַבְעָ֖ם שְׁכֶ֑מָה כִּ֥י שְׁכֶ֛ם בָּ֥אוּ כָל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְהַמְלִ֥יךְ אֹתֽוֹ). The catalog is kept whole on that ground alone -- this book's own coarse treatment of register material -- not on any claim that the wayehi-lamed device itself marks reign-section openings; a finer split at 9-10 | 11-15 on the strength of v11's opener alone remains a live, defensible alternative the boss round may weigh differently. It closes on the hook “עַ֥ד כִּֽי חָזָֽק” (“until he was strong”), the same ḥ-z-q root picked up — as a catchword, not verbatim — at the start of v16's “וּכְחֶזְקָת֗וֹ” (“but when he was strong”), the adjacency (last word of v15, first word of v16) marking the catalog's own terminus despite the differing forms.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this catalog at the building/army seam (9-10 versus 11-15) is the genuine rival: a SAMEKH sits there and v11 opens with the book's own recurring wayehi-lamed-royal-name register-opener. Both are real, but neither carries the force of an actual scene-change device (no time or place shift, no new addressee), so the row keeps the coarse catalog whole rather than multiplying rows inside a single register-type unit -- a call the boss round may revisit.

boundary_rationale: A single root supplies the pivot: v15 just closed on “עַ֥ד כִּֽי חָזָֽק” (“until he was strong”), and v16 opens “וּכְחֶזְקָת֗וֹ גָּבַ֤הּ” (“but when he was strong, his heart was lifted up”), turning the same word into the hinge from success to hubris. The temple trespass, Azariah's confrontation, and the leprosy outbreak run through v21, closing on “וְיוֹתָ֤ם בְּנוֹ֙ עַל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שׁוֹפֵ֖ט אֶת עַ֥ם הָאָֽרֶץ” (“Jotham his son was over the king's house, judging the people of the land”). V22's source-citation formula picks up right where this narrative leaves off.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing the leprosy narrative into the preceding catalog (9-21 as one span) would erase the deliberate verbal echo the text sets up between v15's closing word and v16's opening word.

boundary_rationale: The identical closing device recurs from ch25, this time crediting the record to a named prophet: “וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרֹנִ֑ים כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא” (“Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote”). The death-and-succession formula follows immediately, closing the chapter on “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב עֻזִּיָּ֜הוּ עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו וַיִּקְבְּר֨וּ אֹת֤וֹ עִם אֲבֹתָיו֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יוֹתָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Jotham his son reigned in his place”), the Masoretic tradition's own PE sits after v23 (single-witness, corroborative weight only). 27:1's fresh age-formula for Jotham marks the seam-out.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the source-citation (v22) to the leprosy narrative that precedes it would still leave v22 doing the same work it does everywhere else in the book: opening, not continuing, a reign's closing report. The two-part citation-then-death shape is common but not universal -- 9:29-31 inserts a reign-length figure between them, 16:11-13 an illness notice, 20:34-21:1 an entire fleet episode, 24:25-27 even inverts the order, 33:18-20 wedges in a second source note, 35:26-27 has no death formula follow at all, 36:8 fuses citation and succession into one verse, and 27:7-9 in this very cluster is itself a counter-instance -- so the merge is rejected on the citation formula's own unit-opening force alone, not on a book-wide universal that does not hold.

boundary_rationale: Jotham's reign opens exactly where Uzziah's closed, with the standard age-formula “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יוֹתָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ יְרוּשָׁ֖ה בַּת צָדֽוֹק”, and the evaluation clause that follows measures him against his leprous father rather than against David, closing with the qualifying note “רַ֕ק לֹא בָ֖א אֶל הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה וְע֥וֹד הָעָ֖ם מַשְׁחִיתִֽים” (“however he didn't enter into Yahweh's temple; the people still acted corruptly”) — the temple-entry clause is the pointed echo of Uzziah's own trespass in the preceding chapter, sharing a 17-codepoint run with 26:16's “וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה לְהַקְטִ֖יר” (“he went into Yahweh's temple to burn incense”), broken only by the two verses' differing cantillation on the divine name; the echo is negated here (Jotham did not enter) against Uzziah's own transgressive entry. V3 then opens a fresh building topic with a bare subject pronoun.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the formula straight through the building notices (1-4 combined) would blur the closed evaluation clause, which ends on a specific comparative judgment, against the separate catalog of construction that follows.

boundary_rationale: Three building/tribute notices share a fronted-constituent-plus-qatal achievement register: the gate and wall of Ophel open the row, fronting the independent pronoun, “ה֗וּא בָּנָ֛ה אֶת שַׁ֥עַר בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה הָעֶלְי֑וֹן וּבְחוֹמַ֥ת הָעֹ֛פֶל בָּנָ֖ה לָרֹֽב” (“he built the upper gate of Yahweh's house”); hill-country cities and fortresses follow in v4, fronting the object rather than a pronoun there, tied to v.3 lexically by the repeated building verb rather than by the pronoun pattern; and the Ammonite war-and-tribute notice occupies v5, itself opening with the fronted-pronoun pattern again, “וְ֠הוּא נִלְחַ֞ם” (“he also fought…”). A tier-3 SAMEKH follows v5, single-witness and non-driving, sitting precisely where the register shifts: v6, “וַיִּתְחַזֵּ֖ק יוֹתָ֑ם כִּ֚י הֵכִ֣ין דְּרָכָ֔יו לִפְנֵ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽיו” (“So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before Yahweh his God”), is a verb-initial evaluative summary, not another achievement clause — closer in shape to the piety verdict closing 26:5, “הִצְלִיח֖וֹ הָאֱלֹהִֽים”, than to the building and tribute notices it is grouped with here. The row keeps v6 attached as this catalog's own summary terminus rather than splitting it off, since nothing resumes a narrative after it before the source-citation formula opens v7; but the register shift is real, and the 5/6 seam -- not the 4/5 seam -- is the stronger internal candidate for a split within this catalog.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger rival is not separating v5 from vv3-4 -- both share the fronted-pronoun achievement pattern -- but separating v6's evaluative summary from vv3-5's catalog at the register shift the SAMEKH there corroborates; v6 is kept because it functions as this catalog's own closing verdict rather than opening anything new, but a finer split at 5/6 remains defensible and is left for the boss round.

boundary_rationale: The citation-before-statistic ordering here is not unusual: Solomon's own close runs the identical three-part sequence — citation at 9:29, “וּשְׁאָר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרוֹנִ֑ים”, then a reign-length figure new to the text at 9:30, “וַיִּמְלֹ֨ךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֧ה בִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה”, then death-and-succession at 9:31 — so the standard chronicle formula opening this row, “וְיֶתֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י יוֹתָ֔ם וְכָל מִלְחֲמֹתָ֖יו וּדְרָכָ֑יו הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה” (“the rest of the acts of Jotham...written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah”), yet v8 then restates the same age and reign-length figures given in v1 almost verbatim, “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְחָמֵ֛שׁ שָׁנָ֖ה הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם”, before the death-and-succession formula closes on “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יוֹתָם֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָחָ֥ז בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Ahaz his son reigned in his place”). What is genuinely distinctive is the repetition itself: v8's figures restate what v1 already gave, whereas Solomon's 9:30 reign-length is new information at that point in the text — Jotham's close doubles a statistic already on the record, which Solomon's does not, and unlike Uzziah's close (26:22-23), which states no regnal statistic at all alongside its citation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Assigning v8's restated formula to a row of its own, apart from the citation (v7) and death notice (v9) that bracket it, would treat a three-verse closing complex as if its middle verse were an independent unit despite no scene-change marker separating it from either neighbor.

boundary_rationale: Ahaz receives the book's bluntest evaluation clause among this part's four kings: “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ אָחָ֣ז בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְלֹא עָשָׂ֧ה הַיָּשָׁ֛ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה כְּדָוִ֥יד אָבִֽיו”, immediately followed by an elaborated apostasy catalog rather than the usual brief formula — Baal images, Hinnom-valley child sacrifice, and high-place worship close the row at v4, “וַיְזַבֵּ֧חַ וַיְקַטֵּ֛ר בַּבָּמ֖וֹת וְעַל הַגְּבָע֑וֹת וְתַ֖חַת כָּל עֵ֥ץ רַעֲנָֽן” (“he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places...under every green tree”). The catalog is not a smooth wayyiqtol run: it is broken twice by non-subject-changing disjunctives. V.2 itself closes with a fronted-object-plus-qatal disjunctive, interrupting the wayyiqtol chain v.2's own opening establishes; v.3 then opens with a second disjunctive of a different type, “וְה֥וּא הִקְטִ֖יר” (“Moreover he burned incense”), independent pronoun plus qatal breaking the chain v2's “וַיֵּ֕לֶךְ” sustains, before v3's own wayyiqtol and v4's wayyiqtol pick the chain back up. Neither disjunctive reopens the unit, since neither changes the grammatical subject (Ahaz remains the actor throughout v1-4) nor introduces a new topic, scene, or addressee — it foregrounds one particularly severe act (child sacrifice) within a single catalog of sins under one evaluative heading: throughout vv1-4 there is one actor (Ahaz), one evaluative heading (the negative regnal formula of v.1), and no new addressee or scene at either disjunctive. The row's actual close comes only at v5, which shifts agency from Ahaz as actor to Yahweh as the one who “delivered him” — a genuine change of agency at this particular seam, though not a criterion this row claims to share uniformly with its neighbors: comparable seams elsewhere in this part hold their own subject constant across the seam (M8-2Chr-116's 28:21/22 keeps Ahaz as subject throughout; M8-2Chr-120's 29:2/3, part 3, keeps Hezekiah as subject throughout), so the v.5 shift is argued on its own local terms, not as an instance of a general grammatical-subject-change rule.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this row into the fixed accession pair alone (vv1-2, matching the two-verse pattern at 25:1-2 and 27:1-2) and pushing the apostasy catalog (vv3-4) into its own row would miss that the evaluation clause of vv1-2 is grammatically continuous with, not separate from, the sins that follow: the wayyiqtol chain running through v2-4 (broken twice -- at v.2's own fronted-object disjunctive and at v.3's independent-pronoun disjunctive, both non-subject-changing) completes rather than closes the indictment, so v1-2 and v3-4 read as one unit rather than two.

boundary_rationale: Divine agency takes over as grammatical subject at the row's open, “וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֜הוּ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָיו֮ בְּיַ֣ד מֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָם֒” (“Yahweh his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria”), turning the preceding apostasy catalog into the ground for military disaster at the hands of Aram and Israel. Pekah's slaughter and Zichri's killings of royal officials lead to a captives-and-plunder notice, closing on “וַיָּבִ֥יאוּ אֶת הַשָּׁלָ֖ל לְשֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (“they brought the plunder to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition marks this span densely — SAMEKH breaks fall after v5, v7, and v8 alike (all single-witness, weak corroboration only), so the v8 break cited as the row's close is one of three in this short stretch, not a solitary corroborating signal. V9's existential clause then introduces a new character at that same location.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this judgment report straight into the Oded episode (5-15 as one span) would erase v9's own scene-introducing force: a named participant is brought on, “נָבִ֥יא לַֽיהוָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד שְׁמוֹ֒” (“a prophet of Yahweh...Oded”), followed by a motion verb directed at the army just brought to Samaria, “וַיֵּצֵ֗א.” The seam rests on v.9's own naming-plus-motion construction alone, not on any book-wide sham-hayah ('there was') opener pattern: the only other sham-hayah sequence in 2Chr is 1:3's “כִּי שָׁ֣ם הָיָ֗ה אֹ֤הֶל מוֹעֵד֙ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים”, a subordinate causal clause supplying an inanimate object as background, not a main-clause participant introduction, so the two are not parallel instances of one device.

boundary_rationale: An existential clause introduces the prophet at the same city just named: “וְ֠שָׁם הָיָ֨ה נָבִ֥יא לַֽיהוָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד שְׁמוֹ֒ וַיֵּצֵ֗א” (“but a prophet of Yahweh was there...Oded”), a self-contained scene combining his oracle, the Ephraimite leaders' answering speech (closing v13, “כִּֽי רַבָּ֤ה אַשְׁמָה֙ לָ֔נוּ וַחֲר֥וֹן אָ֖ף עַל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, “our guilt is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel”), and the captives' release. It closes on the return notice “וַיָּשׁ֖וּבוּ שֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (“then they returned to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition also marks two further interior seams — SAMEKH after v11 and after v13 (both single-witness, weak corroboration only) — alongside the boundary-adjacent PE after v15, so the closing mark is one of three in this stretch, not a lone signal. V16's own temporal frame opens an unrelated Assyria episode. The exact edges of this scene remain genuinely debatable, since “Samaria” itself brackets both v8's arrival and v15's return.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating just Oded's speech (9-11) from the leaders' response and the captives' relief (12-15) is not, in fact, a cut with no frame reopening the narrative: v12 opens with a genuine participant-change device, “וַיָּקֻ֨מוּ אֲנָשִׁ֜ים מֵרָאשֵׁ֣י בְנֵֽי אֶפְרַ֗יִם” (“some of the heads of the children of Ephraim...stood up”), naming four new leaders by name — the plural verb itself recurs six times book-wide (20:19, 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 30:14, 30:27), but the sharper pattern this construction actually instances here -- the verb followed by newly-named persons -- stands only at 28:12 and 29:12: 20:19 and 30:27 name only a class of persons, not individuals; 28:15 anaphorically reuses 28:12's own names rather than introducing new ones; and 30:14 expresses no group at all. This narrower count sharpens rather than weakens the parallel this cluster's own decision M8-2Chr-120 draws, which treats the same verb-plus-newly-named-persons pattern as the device that closes a unit at 29:12. What keeps 9-15 together despite that device is the anaphoric envelope the same construction supplies at both ends: v15's identical verb closes the group v12 opens, “וַיָּקֻ֣מוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים֩ אֲשֶׁר נִקְּב֨וּ בְשֵׁמ֜וֹת” (“the men who have been mentioned by name rose up”), naming the same four leaders anaphorically rather than introducing a new party — so the construction here brackets one scene rather than opening a second one, unlike its stand-alone use at 29:12. The merge does not rest on the absence of any frame at v.12 -- a real, named-group-introducing frame exists there -- but on the fact that both of its occurrences, at v.12 and v.15, belong to the same captive-release action rather than opening two separate scenes.

boundary_rationale: A temporal frame opens this row, “בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא שָׁלַ֞ח הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ אָחָ֛ז עַל מַלְכֵ֥י אַשּׁ֖וּר לַעְזֹ֥ר לֽוֹ” (“At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria to help him”), distinct from the scene just closed. Edomite and Philistine invasions follow, and the appeal to Tiglath-Pileser fails, closing on “וַיָּבֹ֣א עָלָ֔יו תִּלְּגַ֥ת פִּלְנְאֶ֖סֶר מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ וְלֹ֥א חֲזָקֽוֹ” (“he gave him trouble, but didn't strengthen him”); v21 then reports Ahaz's own last resort, not a restatement of anything already stated in vv.16-20: כִּֽי חָלַ֤ק אָחָז֙ אֶת בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה וְאֶת בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְהַשָּׂרִ֑ים וַיִּתֵּן֙ לְמֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר וְלֹ֥א לְעֶזְרָ֖ה לֽוֹ (“For Ahaz took away a portion out of Yahweh’s house, and out of the house of the king and of the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria; but it didn’t help him.”) -- Ahaz himself is the agent here, stripping the temple, palace, and officials' own treasuries to pay Assyria, not a report of plunder taken from him; the closing clause seals the failure v.20 already stated, rather than introducing a new defeat. The chapter's actual plunder notice belongs to a different row and a different party: it is the Israelite army's own plunder at 28:8, part of M8-2Chr-114's span, not this one. V22 does not open with a fresh echo of v16's own temporal frame — its distress-clause, “וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ” (“in the time of his distress”), shares only the bare noun 'time' with v16's opener, and instead reproduces v20's own verb root-for-root and suffix-for-suffix, “וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ” (“gave him trouble”) — an anaphor pulling v22 backward into the very Assyria-appeal span it needs to be distinguished from, not a matching frame at the seam; the same idiom recurs independently at 33:12's “וּכְהָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ”, so it is not even unique to this pairing. The real, uncited seam-signal is v22's own closing resumptive naming, “ה֖וּא הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָחָֽז” (“this same King Ahaz”), a full-title reintroduction unattested anywhere else in 2Chr, marking a fresh narrative beat at v22 despite the backward-looking distress-clause that opens it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this Assyria-appeal notice straight through v22-25's further apostasy would erase v22's own resumptive naming, which reintroduces Ahaz by full title in a way the book uses nowhere else -- a stronger, if quieter, seam-signal than the distress-clause it opens with, which is anaphoric to v20 rather than a fresh frame.

boundary_rationale: A matching echo of “time” frames this unit's open, “וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ וַיּ֖וֹסֶף לִמְע֣וֹל בַּיהוָ֑ה” (“in the time of his distress, he trespassed yet more”), pairing against v16's “at that time” to mark a fresh but parallel beat. Sacrifice to Damascus's gods, the cutting-up of temple vessels, and high places in every city of Judah run through the row, closing on “וּבְכָל עִ֨יר וָעִ֤יר לִֽיהוּדָה֙ עָשָׂ֣ה בָמ֔וֹת לְקַטֵּ֖ר לֵֽאלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֑ים וַיַּכְעֵ֕ס אֶת יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבֹתָֽיו” (“he provoked Yahweh, the God of his fathers, to anger”). V26 supplies its own source-citation formula the very next verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the temple-vessel plunder (vv24-25) as a fresh row apart from the Damascus-sacrifice notice (22-23) would split one continuous escalation of trespass that the text narrates without any intervening scene-change marker.

boundary_rationale: The chronicle formula closes the block a fourth time in this part, “וְיֶ֤תֶר דְּבָרָיו֙ וְכָל דְּרָכָ֔יו הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, repeating the dual-kingdom register also used for Amaziah (25:26, the same Judah-then-Israel order) and Jotham (27:7, “עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה”, inverting the order to Israel-then-Judah). This is a construct-phrase device (sefer malkhei X), not a dual-kingdom-content one: a book-wide sweep of the construct phrase finds exactly seven hits (20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), and 20:34 alone among them names Israel only, mediated through Jehu's own record, WEB "Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani, which is included in the book of the kings of Israel." -- not the dual-kingdom phrasing the register argument needs. The book's true dual-kingdom phrase is a different construction, Asa's own closing citation at 16:11, WEB "Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.", a definite-article-plus-lamed construction excluded from this seven-hit construct-phrase count on form rather than content. Uzziah's own closing citation at 26:22, “כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא” (WEB “Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote.”), is a different device, a prophetic-authorship citation naming no book of kings at all, and does not belong to this register: a book-wide sweep finds the register phrase at exactly seven verses (20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), 26:22 not among them. The death-and-succession formula follows, closing this part's final verse on Ahaz's denial of the royal tombs proper, “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב אָחָ֜ז עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֤הוּ בָעִיר֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֻ֔הוּ לְקִבְרֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְחִזְקִיָּ֥הֽוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“because they didn't bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel”), corroborated by a PE mark following v27 (single-witness).
